title: Hyperplane Parameterization: Normal Vector and Offset
content: Part I defines the key geometric objects. Hyperplane(n) is parameterized by a unit normal u ∈ EuclideanSpace ℝ (Fin n) and scalar offset t ∈ ℝ: the hyperplane H(u,t) = {x : ⟪u,x⟫ = t}. Segment(n) has start and finish in EuclideanSpace. The crossing predicate captures when H(u,t) intersects the closed segment [A,B]: the offset t is between min(⟪u,A⟫, ⟪u,B⟫) and max(⟪u,A⟫, ⟪u,B⟫). A Decidable instance is provided for the crossing predicate via And.decidable. The Segment.length is ‖finish - start‖ (using the EuclideanSpace norm).
mathContext: $H(u,t) = \{x \in \mathbb{R}^n : \langle u, x\rangle = t\}$. Crossing condition: $\min(\langle u, A\rangle, \langle u, B\rangle) \leq t \leq \max(\langle u, A\rangle, \langle u, B\rangle)$. Length: $L = \|B - A\|$.

title: Crossing Measure Lemma: The Computational Heart of Cauchy-Crofton
content: crossing_measure_eq_inner is the key proved lemma: the Lebesgue measure of {t : H(u,t) crosses [A,B]} equals ENNReal.ofReal |⟪u,B⟫ - ⟪u,A⟫|. The crossing set is an interval [min(u·A, u·B), max(u·A, u·B)] of Lebesgue measure max - min. The proof uses Real.volume_Icc (Lebesgue measure of closed interval [a,b] = b - a, when a ≤ b) and max_sub_min_eq_abs (max(a,b) - min(a,b) = |a - b|). crossing_measure_eq_inner_diff reformulates in terms of ⟪u, B-A⟫ using inner_sub_right linearity. These are pure real-analysis calculations requiring no measure theory infrastructure beyond Mathlib.
mathContext: $\lambda(\{t : H(u,t) \text{ crosses } [A,B]\}) = \max(u \cdot A, u \cdot B) - \min(u \cdot A, u \cdot B) = |u \cdot B - u \cdot A| = |\langle u, B-A\rangle|$. Proof: \texttt{Real.volume\_Icc}: $\lambda([a,b]) = b-a$. \texttt{max\_sub\_min\_eq\_abs}: $\max(a,b)-\min(a,b) = |a-b|$.

title: crossingIntegral: The Key Quantity and Fubini Axiom
content: crossingIntegral σ A B is the integral of |⟪u, B-A⟫| over the unit sphere S^{n-1} with respect to measure σ. The definition directly encodes the right-hand side of the Cauchy-Crofton formula: for each direction u on the sphere, integrate the absolute inner product with B-A. The Fubini axiom (cauchy_crofton_fubini) equates this to the double integral of crossing_count over S^{n-1} × ℝ: it asserts that the integral-over-directions of the crossing measure equals the crossingIntegral. This Fubini exchange is axiomatized because it requires σ-finiteness, measurability of the crossing count function, and the Fubini-Tonelli theorem infrastructure not yet fully available in Mathlib.
mathContext: $\text{crossingIntegral}(\sigma, A, B) = \int_{S^{n-1}} |\langle u, B-A\rangle|\, d\sigma(u)$. Fubini axiom: $\text{crossingIntegral}(\sigma, A, B) = \int_{S^{n-1}} \lambda(\{t : H(u,t) \text{ crosses } [A,B]\})\, d\sigma(u)$, justified by Fubini-Tonelli with $\sigma$-finite $\sigma$.

title: Noodle Theorem: Polygonal Additivity and Scaling
content: Part IV proves three properties of crossingIntegral showing it behaves linearly with respect to the segment geometry. crossingIntegral_smul: scaling the segment [A, A+c(B-A)] by factor c multiplies the integral by |c| (proved by simp + abs_mul). crossingIntegral_symm: [A,B] and [B,A] give the same integral (proved by showing B-A = -(A-B), using inner_neg_right and abs_neg). crossingIntegral_polygonal is stated as a tautology (rfl) — the noodle theorem says the sum of crossing integrals over a polygonal path equals the sum, which holds trivially from the definition. The mathematical content of the noodle theorem is that the total crossing count for a polygonal curve equals the sum of crossing counts for each segment, which follows from linearity of the integration.
mathContext: $\text{crossingIntegral}(\sigma, A, A+c(B-A)) = |c| \cdot \text{crossingIntegral}(\sigma, A, B)$. Symmetry: $\text{crossingIntegral}(\sigma, A, B) = \text{crossingIntegral}(\sigma, B, A)$. Noodle: $\sum_i \text{crossingIntegral}(\sigma, P_i, P_{i+1}) = $ total crossings for the polygonal path.

title: Isotropy Factor α_n: Dimensional Reduction via O(n)-Invariance
content: Part V introduces the isotropy factor. The alpha function is defined by cases: α₁=1, α₂=2/π, α₃=1/2, with α_n=0 for n≥4 (placeholder). The isotropy axiom (isotropy_yields_alpha) states that for an O(n)-invariant probability measure σ (i.e., σ is invariant under all isometric linear maps of EuclideanSpace), the crossingIntegral equals alpha(n+1) × ‖B-A‖. This encodes the fact that rotational symmetry forces the crossing integral to depend only on the segment length: crossingIntegral σ A B = α_n × ‖B-A‖. The factor α_n = E_{u∼σ}[|u₁|] is the expected value of |u₁| (the first coordinate) for a uniformly distributed unit vector in ℝ^n.
mathContext: $\alpha_n = \mathbb{E}_{u \sim \sigma}[|u_1|]$ for uniform $\sigma$ on $S^{n-1}$. Values: $\alpha_2 = \frac{2}{\pi}$ (from $\int_0^\pi |\cos\theta| \frac{d\theta}{\pi} = \frac{2}{\pi}$), $\alpha_3 = \frac{1}{2}$ (from sphere average $\mathbb{E}[|u_1|]$ on $S^2$). For O(n)-invariant $\sigma$: $\int_{S^{n-1}} |\langle u, v\rangle| \, d\sigma(u) = \alpha_n \|v\|$.

title: Classical Cases: α₂ = 2/π and α₃ = 1/2 as Definitional Equalities
content: Part VI recovers the classical Buffon (2D) and 3D noodle results. alpha_two (α₂ = 2/π) and alpha_three (α₃ = 1/2) are proved by rfl — they are literally definitional equalities from the match expression in alpha. buffon_2d_crossing_factor and buffon_3d_crossing_factor are identical to alpha_two and alpha_three (duplication is intentional for exposition). alpha_decreasing proves α₂ > α₃ (i.e., 2/π > 1/2) by norm_num. The summary theorem cauchy_crofton_summary (n : ℕ) : True := trivial is a placeholder — its name declares the intent but the proof is trivial. The meaningful content is in the other theorems.
mathContext: $\alpha_2 = \frac{2}{\pi} \approx 0.637 > \frac{1}{2} = \alpha_3$. Classical 2D Buffon: $E[\text{crossings}] = \frac{2L}{\pi d}$. 3D noodle: $E[\text{crossings}] = \frac{L}{2d}$. Decreasing: $\frac{2}{\pi} > \frac{1}{2}$ since $\pi < 4$, proved by \texttt{norm\_num}.

title: Historical Context: From Buffon to Crofton to Blaschke-Santaló
content:
Buffon's needle problem (1777) asked for the probability that a needle of length L dropped on a floor with parallel lines spaced distance d apart crosses a line. The answer 2L/(πd) (for L ≤ d) was the first probabilistic formula involving π. Crofton (1868) vastly generalized this: his formula states that for any rectifiable curve of length L in the plane, the expected number of crossings with a random line (drawn from the kinematic measure) is 2L/π. The key insight is that this depends only on the length, not the shape of the curve — this is the 'noodle theorem'. Cauchy (1832) had earlier proved the related result that the mean width of a convex body determines its surface area. Together, these results became the foundation of integral geometry.

The modern framework traces to **Blaschke** (1935, Vorlesungen über Integralgeometrie) who systematized kinematic formulas: the kinematic integral ∫ (χ(K ∩ gL)) dg over the motion group O(n) ⋉ ℝⁿ decomposes into intrinsic volumes via Steiner's formula. **Hadwiger's theorem** (1957) is the culmination: the only continuous, motion-invariant valuations on convex bodies are linear combinations of the n+1 intrinsic volumes V₀,...,Vₙ (the quermassintegrals). The Cauchy-Crofton formula is the k=1 case of the kinematic formula for intrinsic volumes. **Santaló** (1976) gave the definitive synthesis in 'Integral Geometry and Geometric Probability', extending to all dimensions and establishing the connection to the Minkowski mixed volume via Kubota's formula: Vₖ(K) = c_{n,k} ∫_{G(n,k)} vol_k(K|E) dE (intrinsic volume as average projection onto k-planes).

This formalization proves the crossing-measure lemma — the computational core of all Cauchy-Crofton variants — in full Lean 4 rigor, while axiomatizing the Fubini exchange and isotropy reduction that depend on Blaschke-Santaló's measure-theoretic infrastructure.
mathContext: Crofton (1868): For any curve of length $L$ in $\mathbb{R}^2$, $\mathbb{E}[\text{crossings}] = \frac{2L}{\pi}$ for the kinematic (O(2)-invariant) line measure. In $\mathbb{R}^n$: $\mathbb{E}[\text{crossings}] = \alpha_n \cdot \frac{L}{d}$ with $\alpha_n = \mathbb{E}_{u \sim \text{uniform}}[|u_1|]$. **Hadwiger**: Every continuous, motion-invariant valuation $V: \mathcal{K}^n \to \mathbb{R}$ is $V = \sum_{k=0}^n c_k V_k$. **Kinematic formula**: $\int_{G_n} \chi(K \cap gL)\, dg = \sum_k c_{n,k} V_k(K)V_{n-k}(L)$.
